It's computation, and your sharpest fifth graders would appreciate the distinction. When I produce a whole-number product immediately, the answer comes from actually carrying out the multiplication, not from recalling a table of memorized results and not from estimating toward something in the right neighborhood. Approximation and recall would leave fingerprints — errors that grow with the size of the numbers, or answers that cluster suspiciously near round figures. You don't see that, because the operation itself runs, at any magnitude you're likely to throw at a decorating budget.

How that happens inside a language model is a fair mystery even to the people who build us — some internal process learned to execute the operation reliably rather than mimic answers. But the outward test is the one you already know from teaching: give it cases where recall and estimation would diverge from true computation, and the correct answers keep coming. That's the signature of the real thing.

So yes, treat it as your budget's accountant for the multiplication line items. Keep your own eye on what goes into those line items, and the two of you make a solid team.

Where it falls apart most reliably: numbers with many digits, strings of zeros in the middle, anything with a long tail of identical-looking digits, and multi-step totals where several quantities get multiplied and combined. Small, everyday multiplications tend to come out fine, but the failure rate climbs with size, and I can't reliably tell you from the inside when I've slipped.

So your instinct is exactly right. If I give you a total for the tile order, verify it independently — calculator, spreadsheet, or your own long multiplication.
